newsitem.title: USA: U.S. housing starts rebound weakly in January.
newsitem.headline: U.S. housing starts rebound weakly in January.

text.p: Construction starts on new homes and apartments rose only slightly in January, the Commerce Department said on Thursday, as the housing sector showed signs of leveling off from a booming 1996.

Building starts were up just 2 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.35 million last month -- well under the 1.42-million-unit rate economists had anticipated -- after a revised 11 percent plunge in December.

Weather was a factor in the December building slump, notably in the West where floods and cold hit the region, but analysts said the weak January bounce-back indicated 1997 was likely to see waning construction activity.
"There's going to be a modest, orderly slowdown in housing from an unsustainable level in 1996," said economist David Seiders of the National Association of Home Builders.
Seiders said building starts likely will ease down by about 6 percent to 1.38 million this year from 1.47 million in 1996.
Mortgage rates remain relatively low by historical standards, which is expected to sustain construction and sales of new and existing homes and prevent any big drop in building.
But overall economic activity is widely expected to moderate as the economy enters a seventh year of expansion in March.
Economists caution that Federal Reserve policy makers are poised to raise interest rates if they foresee that tight labour markets risk fuelling inflationary price rises.

"The economic fundamentals, such as confidence about employment, won't grow as rapidly this year and also we expect (Federal Reserve) Chairman (Alan) Greenspan to hike interest rates in 1997, so that will impair housing," said economist Sung Won Sohn of Norwest Corp. in Minneapolis.
"Housing has probably seen its best years," Sohn said.

In a separate report Thursday, the Labour Department said there was a small rise in the number of Americans filing first-time claims for jobless pay last week. There were 309,000 claims filed in the week ended Saturday, up 1,000 from a week earlier.

But the four-week moving average for claims, which smoothes out the weekly numbers, fell last week to 318,250 from a revised 325,500 a week earlier. That implies continued strong job opportunities despite the rise in claims last week.
Housing plays a key role in the national economy since it influences everything from employment to manufacturing of building materials and retail sales of products used to equip and furnish a home.
Its performance in January was a mixed one.

Building starts on single-family homes were up 10.2 percent to a rate of 1.11 million a year after dropping 11.3 percent in December. But starts on apartments plummeted 23.9 percent to 242,000 a year after a 9.9 percent drop in December.

Regionally in January, starts in the West climbed 29.8 percent to a rate of 344,000 a year, more than recovering from a 25.6 percent decline in December. In the Northeast, starts shot up 22.2 percent to 165,000 a year, the strongest building rate since 176,000 in November 1994.
But in the Midwest, January starts fell sharply by 13.2 percent to 256,000 a year and in the South -- the largest regional market -- they fell 6.8 percent to 585,000 a year.

New applications for building permits were down 1.9 percent to 1.395 million a year last month after a slim 0.3 percent gain in December, indicating the construction activity may be muted in coming months.
Previously, the department said December building starts had fallen 12.2 percent to a rate of 1.329 million a year but it revised that estimate upward.
January starts were 6.5 percent lower than a year earlier, when ground was being broken for new homes and apartments at a rate of 1.444 million a year.
A return of more favourable spring weather and some recent easing in mortgage rates may bolster building activity.

The Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp., or Freddie Mac, said rates for a 30-year loan averaged 7.65 percent in the week ending Feb. 14, down from 7.74 percent last week. The rate was the lowest since 7.64 percent in the week ended Dec. 27.
